a2Note: 33 kW (45 PS) and 165 kg fully fuelled sit exactly on the A2 power and power-to-weight limits; sold as an A2 model in Europe.
beginnerNote: Light, slim and A2-legal with friendly electronics, but the eager single and sharp chassis reward a bit of restraint — a great first bike for a committed learner rather than a nervous one.
whoFor: New or A2 riders who want the sharpest, most grown-up-feeling small naked — urban scratching in the week, twisty backroads at the weekend.
notFor: Maybe not for you if you regularly carry a passenger or need wind protection for motorway miles.
about: The third-generation 390 Duke (2024 onwards) is 90% new, with a 398.7 cc single, a stiffer trellis frame, an off-centre WP shock and the distinctive split LED headlight. It packs a 5-inch TFT dash, ride modes, cornering ABS with Supermoto mode and launch control — equipment unheard of in the class. At 165 kg fully fuelled with 45 hp, it is one of the quickest-steering, most engaging A2 machines on sale.
pros: Class-leading electronics (TFT, ride modes, cornering ABS)
Very light and agile — 165 kg fully fuelled
Strong 45 hp single uses the full A2 allowance
15 l tank gives real-world range for a small naked
Adjustable WP APEX suspension
cons: Firm seat and no wind protection on longer rides
Single-cylinder vibration at sustained motorway speeds

a2Note: 33 kW (45 PS) and 176 kg fully fuelled — comfortably inside A2 power-to-weight limits.
beginnerNote: Upright ergonomics, an 825 mm seat that is low for the class, smooth power and generous suspension travel make this one of the friendliest ways into adventure biking.
whoFor: New and A2 riders who want one do-it-all bike — daily commuting, light touring and the occasional gravel road — without big-bike weight or cost.
notFor: Maybe not for you if you want serious off-road ability (the spoked-wheel 390 Adventure R is the harder-core sibling) or strong motorway overtaking reserve.
about: The 2025-generation 390 Adventure was redesigned around the new LC4c 399 cc single, with rally-inspired bodywork, a 19/17-inch cast wheel setup and 200 mm of WP APEX travel at both ends. The X trim keeps the essentials — ride modes, offroad ABS, TFT dash and a windscreen — at a sharp price. It is light, economical and unintimidating, yet genuinely capable on rough tracks.
pros: 200 mm suspension travel and 232 mm ground clearance
Friendly 45 hp delivery with offroad ABS and ride modes
Accessible 825 mm seat and light 176 kg wet weight
Excellent value for an adventure-styled A2 bike
Rally-style bodywork with usable wind protection
cons: Cast 19/17 wheels and road-biased tyres limit hard off-roading
Single cylinder runs out of breath at motorway pace
Basic (non-adjustable) suspension on the X trim
14 l tank is adequate rather than generous for touring

a2Note: Homologated at exactly 35 kW with 175 kg wet weight — Aprilia markets it as the best power-to-weight ratio available on an A2 licence.
beginnerNote: Deliberately designed for A2 riders — smooth ride-by-wire twin, slipper clutch, traction control and unintimidating power — though the sporty crouch and track focus suit an enthusiastic learner more than a pure commuter.
whoFor: A2 riders who dream of the RSV4 and want the most genuinely sporty small sportbike — aluminium frame, real electronics and track-day credibility included.
notFor: Maybe not for you if you prioritise comfort, pillion space or upright ergonomics over cornering feel.
about: The RS 457 is Aprilia's ground-up A2 sportbike: a 457 cc parallel twin producing 35 kW in a dual-beam aluminium frame — chassis architecture borrowed from its supersport heritage and rare in this class. It carries ride-by-wire with three riding modes, traction control, dual-map ABS and a 5-inch TFT. At 175 kg wet with 47.6 hp, it is one of the quickest and best-handling bikes a new licence holder can buy.
pros: Aluminium twin-spar frame — unique at this price point
Class-leading power-to-weight for A2
Full electronics suite: ride modes, traction control, dual-map ABS
Characterful 270-degree parallel twin with slipper clutch
Genuine track-day ability with approachable manners
cons: Committed riding position tires on long commutes

a2Note: Far above the 35 kW A2 ceiling and cannot legally be restricted (base power exceeds 70 kW).
beginnerNote: A 210 hp, 303 km/h homologated superbike is emphatically not a first motorcycle, however sophisticated its electronics safety net.
whoFor: Experienced sport riders and track-day regulars who want a WorldSBK-derived flagship that is still remarkably rideable on the road.
notFor: Maybe not for you if you commute, tour two-up, or hold anything less than full confidence in your throttle discipline.
about: BMW's flagship superbike pairs a 999 cc ShiftCam inline-four making 210 hp with winglets, a 6.5-inch TFT and one of the deepest electronics packages in production motorcycling — seven riding modes, cornering ABS Pro, slide control and a pit-lane limiter. The latest update added the M quick-action throttle and Brake Slide Assist from the M 1000 RR. It laps circuits with world-class pace yet remains more forgiving than its numbers suggest.
pros: 210 hp ShiftCam engine with immense, flexible delivery
Benchmark electronics: Race Pro modes, slide control, launch control, pit limiter
Standard bidirectional Shift Assistant Pro
Aerodynamic winglets and Brake Slide Assist from the M programme
Surprisingly civil ergonomics for a superbike
cons: Superbike ergonomics punish long road stints
Expensive once M package and options are added
Performance is unusable on public roads without restraint
